provenance.method: lesson notes written from the NERDC 2025 scheme of work outline; every week keeps its scheme topic and bullets as the teaching spine

topics.title: WAEC marathon: final accounts
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to state the components of final accounts, explain the purpose of each component, and solve past questions on final accounts.

Introduction:
We have learned about the accounting cycle and how to prepare the trial balance. Today we will practice WAEC past questions on final accounts to prepare for the examination.

Content:
Final accounts consist of the trading account, profit and loss account, and balance sheet. The trading account shows gross profit or loss, calculated as sales minus cost of goods sold. For example, if a market trader buys goods for N50,000 and sells for N80,000, the gross profit is N30,000. The profit and loss account shows net profit after deducting all expenses like rent, salaries, and depreciation. The balance sheet shows the financial position at a specific date, with assets equal to liabilities plus capital.

Class activity:
Students will work in groups to solve three past WAEC questions on final accounts within 40 minutes.

Evaluation questions:
1. List the components of final accounts.
2. State the formula for calculating gross profit.
3. Differentiate between trading account and profit and loss account.
4. A business has sales of N200,000, purchases of N120,000, and expenses of N30,000. Calculate the net profit.

Summary:
Final accounts are essential for showing business performance and financial position, and practice with past questions improves exam readiness.

topics.title: WAEC marathon: adjustments
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify necessary adjustments, explain the purpose of each adjustment, and solve past questions on adjustments.

Introduction:
We have studied the types of adjustments in accounting. Today we will practice WAEC past questions involving adjustments to financial statements.

Content:
Adjustments are made to ensure accounts reflect the true financial position. Common adjustments include prepaid expenses, accrued income, depreciation, provision for bad debts, and inventory valuation. For example, if rent of N12,000 is paid annually and three months have passed, N3,000 should be recognized as expense with N9,000 as prepaid expense. Similarly, if a delivery van costs N1,000,000 with a useful life of 5 years, annual depreciation would be N200,000 using straight-line method.

Class activity:
Students will work in pairs to complete a worksheet with various adjustment scenarios and prepare adjusted financial statements.

Evaluation questions:
1. List four types of adjustments in final accounts.
2. Explain the purpose of depreciation in financial statements.
3. A business paid N60,000 for insurance annually on January 1. Prepare the adjustment on December 31.
4. Differentiate between accrued expenses and prepaid expenses.

Summary:
Adjustments are crucial for accurate financial reporting and practicing past questions helps master this important topic.

topics.title: WAEC marathon: partnership
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to state the features of a partnership, explain the distribution of profits, and solve past questions on partnership accounts.

Introduction:
We have learned about partnership formation and accounting principles. Today we will practice WAEC past questions on partnership accounts to strengthen our understanding.

Content:
A partnership is a business owned by two or more people who share profits and losses. Partnership accounts include the appropriation account, which shows how profits are distributed. Partners may receive interest on capital, salaries, and share remaining profits in their agreed ratio. For example, if A and B contribute N200,000 and N300,000 respectively and share profits 60:40, and both receive 10% interest on capital, with N50,000 salary to A, the profit distribution can be calculated accordingly.

Class activity:
Students will work in groups to solve partnership accounting problems involving profit distribution and admission of a new partner.

Evaluation questions:
1. List three features of a partnership.
2. Explain the purpose of the appropriation account.
3. A and B are partners with capital balances of N150,000 and N100,000 respectively. They share profits equally. Prepare the profit distribution if profit is N80,000 and both partners receive 5% interest on capital.
4. Differentiate between fixed and fluctuating capital accounts.

Summary:
Partnership accounting requires careful distribution of profits and practice with past questions enhances exam performance.

topics.title: Mock examination
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to complete a full mock examination paper within the time limit, apply accounting principles to solve problems, and evaluate their performance.

Introduction:
We have covered various accounting topics throughout the term. Today we will take a full mock examination to assess our readiness for the WAEC exam.

Content:
The mock examination will cover all major accounting topics including final accounts, adjustments, partnership, control accounts, and incomplete records. Students will have 2 hours 30 minutes to complete the paper, which consists of theory and practical questions. The paper will follow the WAEC format with multiple choice, theory, and problem-solving sections. For example, a practical question might require students to prepare a set of final accounts from a trial balance and additional information.

Class activity:
Students will write the full mock examination under exam conditions. After completion, papers will be collected and marked by the teacher.

Evaluation questions:
The mock examination itself serves as evaluation with questions covering all topics taught in the term.

Summary:
The mock examination provides valuable practice for the WAEC exam and helps identify areas needing improvement.

topics.title: Weakness clinics
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify their weak areas in accounting, explain concepts they found challenging, and solve targeted problems to improve.

Introduction:
After the mock examination, we have identified areas where students need additional practice. Today we will focus on these weak areas through targeted drills.

Content:
Weakness clinics will focus on topics where students performed poorly in the mock exam. Common areas include complex adjustments, partnership profit distribution, and control accounts. For each topic, the teacher will provide additional explanations and examples. For instance, if students struggled with provision for bad debts, the teacher will explain different methods of calculating bad debts and provide worked examples. Students will then practice similar problems to reinforce understanding.

Class activity:
Students will work in small groups on worksheets focusing on their identified weak areas, with the teacher providing guidance as needed.

Evaluation questions:
1. Explain one concept you found challenging in the mock exam.
2. Solve this problem: A business has trade receivables of N500,000. It is decided to create a provision of 5% for doubtful debts. Show the journal entry and effect on the final accounts.
3. How has this clinic helped improve your understanding of difficult topics?

Summary:
Targeted practice on weak areas helps overcome difficulties and improves overall accounting performance.

topics.title: Speed and accuracy
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to solve accounting problems quickly, maintain accuracy under time pressure, and track their improvement in speed and precision.

Introduction:
In the WAEC exam, students must complete many questions within limited time. Today we will practice improving our speed and accuracy in solving accounting problems.

Content:
Speed and accuracy are crucial for exam success. Students will practice objective questions and short problems within timed intervals. For example, students might have 10 minutes to solve 10 multiple choice questions on adjustments or 15 minutes to prepare a trading account from given data. The teacher will emphasize techniques for quick calculation, such as using shortcuts for depreciation calculations or standard formats for final accounts. Students will track their scores to monitor improvement over time.

Class activity:
Students will participate in timed rounds of objective questions and short problems, recording their scores for each round to track progress.

Evaluation questions:
1. Solve these 5 questions in 5 minutes: a) What is the purpose of a suspense account? b) List two types of depreciation. c) Calculate gross profit: Sales N300,000, Purchases N180,000, Closing stock N30,000. d) State two features of a partnership. e) What is the formula for calculating cost of goods sold?
2. How can you improve your speed in solving accounting problems?
3. What strategies help maintain accuracy when working quickly?

Summary:
Developing speed and accuracy through timed practice is essential for success in the WAEC examination.

topics.title: Project: full set of accounts
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to prepare a complete set of accounts from source documents, explain the accounting process, and submit accurate work.

Introduction:
Throughout this term, we have learned various aspects of accounting. Today you will apply this knowledge by preparing a full set of accounts for a business scenario.

Content:
For this project, students will receive a package of source documents including invoices, receipts, bank statements, and other records for a small business. They will need to record all transactions in the books of original entry, post to the ledger, prepare a trial balance, make necessary adjustments, and prepare final accounts including trading, profit and loss, and balance sheet. For example, a local food vendor's records might include purchases of ingredients, sales records, payment for rent, and equipment purchases. Students must apply proper accounting principles throughout the process.

Class activity:
Students will work individually to complete the accounting project, submitting their work at the end of the week for assessment.

Evaluation questions:
1. List the books of original entry you used in this project.
2. Explain the process you followed to prepare the final accounts.
3. What challenges did you encounter in completing this project?
4. How does this project help prepare you for the WAEC exam?

Summary:
Completing a full set of accounts reinforces all accounting concepts and prepares students for the practical aspects of the examination.

topics.title: Final mock
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to complete a full examination paper under exam conditions, demonstrate mastery of all accounting topics, and finalize their preparation.

Introduction:
We are in the final week before the WAEC examination. Today we will take our last full mock exam to ensure we are fully prepared.

Content:
The final mock examination will be a comprehensive paper covering all accounting topics likely to appear in the WAEC exam. Students will have 2 hours 30 minutes to complete the paper following strict exam conditions. The paper will include multiple choice questions, theory questions, and practical problems of varying difficulty. For example, a practical question might require students to prepare financial statements for a partnership with complex profit-sharing arrangements or solve a problem involving incomplete records.

Class activity:
Students will write the examination under supervised conditions. After submission, papers will be marked and returned with feedback.

Evaluation questions:
The final mock examination itself serves as evaluation with questions covering all accounting topics.

Summary:
The final mock exam provides comprehensive practice and helps students feel confident and prepared for the actual WAEC examination.

topics.title: WAEC readiness
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain effective exam strategies, demonstrate proper exam techniques, and approach the WAEC examination with confidence.

Introduction:
The WAEC examination is approaching. Today we will focus on exam strategies and techniques to ensure success.

Content:
Effective exam strategies include time management, question analysis, and presentation of answers. Students should allocate time based on marks available, spending more time on higher-value questions. For example, in a 2-hour 30-minute exam with 100 marks, students should aim to spend about 1 minute per mark. They should read all questions carefully, highlighting key terms and requirements. Answers should be structured clearly with proper headings and workings shown. Students should also prepare necessary materials like mathematical sets, calculators, and wristwatches.

Class activity:
Students will participate in a discussion about exam strategies and create a personal exam preparation checklist.

Evaluation questions:
1. List three strategies for effective time management during the exam.
2. Explain how you should approach a theory question requiring an explanation.
3. What materials should you bring to the examination hall?
4. How can you stay calm during the examination?

Summary:
Proper preparation and exam strategies help students perform their best in the WAEC examination.
